justification_text:
My probabilistic forecast centered on a consistent point estimate of 119.61 across all time horizons – one day, one week, and one month. This uniformity indicates that, based on the information available at the time of the forecast, 119.61 was assessed as the most probable outcome, representing a current equilibrium or baseline value. There were no strong indicators suggesting a significant directional shift (up or down) was more likely over any of these specific periods, leading to the expectation that the value would naturally gravitate around this level in the absence of major unforeseen catalysts.

The widening of the 90% confidence intervals for each successive horizon directly reflects the inherent increase in uncertainty over time. For the one-day forecast, the tight interval of [117.25, 121.97] primarily accounts for typical daily market fluctuations and minor movements. As we extend to one week, the interval expands to [114.33, 124.89], acknowledging that more opportunities arise for normal volatility, minor shifts in underlying conditions, or the cumulative effect of small daily changes to influence the outcome. The one-month interval, stretching from [108.06, 130.17], captures the most significant uncertainty, as over a longer duration, a greater number of variables can come into play and compound, making the precise future value less predictable within a narrower range.

Specific risks or unforeseen events could certainly push outcomes beyond these stated intervals. These would typically involve major disruptions or shifts not fully incorporated into the baseline assumptions. Examples include sudden, drastic changes in economic policy, unexpected geopolitical conflicts or resolutions, or significant macroeconomic shocks like a severe recession or unexpected inflationary spike. On a more localized level, major unanticipated news concerning the underlying asset, such as a major earnings surprise, a significant regulatory change, or a disruptive technological breakthrough, could also lead to outcomes falling outside the forecasted 90% ranges, representing the "tail risks" that are inherently difficult to quantify within standard probabilistic models.
